$comment: The Uniswap Hooks Security Framework, expressed as data.
This is a faithful port of the framework's prose into a form a program can
evaluate. Where the prose is unambiguous, this file reproduces it. Where it
is not, this file makes an interpretation and marks it `interpretation: true`
with a pointer to the FEEDBACK.md item that reports the gap upstream.
That distinction is the whole point. A scoring tool that silently invents
definitions produces numbers that look like the framework's and are not. Every
value below is either the Foundation's or visibly ours.
The Uniswap Foundation does not review, endorse or certify this port, nor any
score derived from it. See the disclaimer in their README.
$comment_strengths: The framework uses five words for recommendation strength and never orders
them, so multiple triggers firing on one hook produce conflicting guidance
with no stated resolution. FEEDBACK.md #3 reports this.
We define the ordinal below and merge by maximum. `required` and `mandatory`
are treated as the same level: they appear interchangeably in the source and
we found no case where a distinction was intended.
$comment_dimensions: Only TVL potential and Team maturity carry brackets in the source. For the
other seven we derived brackets from the descriptive prose; each is marked
`bracketsAreInterpretation: true`. FEEDBACK.md #2 asks the Foundation to
publish authoritative ones, at which point ours should be deleted.
`measurable` records whether hookrisk can observe the value from code and
chain state, or whether it must be declared by the team. A measured value and
a declared value are not the same kind of claim and the manifest keeps them

dimensions.name: Complexity
dimensions.description: Total code complexity including branching logic, number of callbacks, configuration patterns, and multi-step flows.
dimensions.interpretationNote: Derived from callback count, hook state written in callbacks, external calls in the swap path, returns-delta and privileged surface — the properties the source's prose names and the hook-profile classification can count. See FEEDBACK.md #2.

brackets.label: No callbacks implemented; pass-through only
1-2 callbacks, no hook state written in them
Callbacks write hook state, or 3+ callbacks
Returns a delta, or makes an external call in the swap path
Returns a delta and makes an external call in the swap path
Returns a delta, external call in the swap path, and an owner-only surface

$comment_derivation: How hookrisk turns the `hook-profile` classification's metrics into a
score. Evaluated highest score first; the first rule whose `when` holds
wins. `when` uses the same tiny grammar as requirement conditions
(`name OP number`, bare boolean names, `&&` / `||`, left to right, no
parentheses), over the metric names the engine-metadata contract defines.
This is an interpretation: the framework describes complexity in prose
and publishes no brackets. The rationale per rule says which sentence of
that prose the rule reads. HS-01 / HS-02 findings still establish a floor

rules.rationale: Custom settlement, a mid-swap dependency and a privileged surface together are every source of 'multi-step flows' and 'configuration patterns' the prose lists.
A hook that both alters settled amounts and leaves the swap path mid-flight has two interacting flows to reason about, not one.
Either a returns-delta permission or an external call in the swap path is a 'multi-step flow' in the prose's sense: the callback's effect is not local to itself.
Hook state written in callbacks is the 'branching logic' the prose names first; three or more callbacks is its 'number of callbacks'.
One or two callbacks that write no hook state: observers and pass-through guards.
Nothing to branch on. A hook contract with no callback implemented is pass-through by construction.

dimensions.name: Custom math
dimensions.description: Any math deviating from standard constant-product AMM operations: custom bonding curves, dynamic fee formulas, TWAMM or streaming-swap math, non-integer exponents, logarithmic or exponential functions, composite pricing, weighted or piecewise curves, multi-variable state transformations.
dimensions.interpretationNote: Ordered by the failure modes the source lists: rounding drift, then input-range violations, then discontinuities, then invariant instability.

brackets.label: No arithmetic beyond bookkeeping
Fixed-point multiply/divide with audited libraries only
Fee or weight formulas over pool state
A custom curve or invariant function
Time-dependent or iterative math (TWAMM, streaming, decay)
Non-integer exponents, logarithms, or piecewise/discontinuous curves

dimensions.name: External dependencies
dimensions.description: Oracles, lending markets, LST systems, bridges, cross-chain flows, off-chain data sources.

brackets.label: None; the hook touches only the PoolManager and the pair's tokens
One immutable, trusted dependency read outside the swap path
A dependency read inside the swap path, or more than one dependency
Cross-chain or off-chain data, or a dependency that can be replaced

$comment_findingDerivation: HS-05 reports one finding per external call inside the swap path whose
destination is neither the PoolManager nor one of the pair's tokens.
The score depends on the call's kind, which the detector carries on the
finding as `metrics.isStatic`. Rules are read in the order written; the
first whose class and condition match wins, and a rule with no `when`
is that class's fallback.
Silence does not measure this dimension. HS-05 never looks outside the
swap path, and 'one immutable, trusted dependency read outside the swap
path' is the framework's own 1 bracket — so a hook with an oracle read
in afterInitialize and none in beforeSwap is a 1 that HS-05 cannot see.

rules.rationale: A staticcall inside the swap path cannot write to the dependency or reenter the PoolManager, so the swap depends on the dependency's value but not on its behaviour. Scored 1, 'one immutable, trusted dependency', as a floor: the framework's 2 bracket says 'a dependency read inside the swap path' without qualifying the call kind, so a reviewer who finds the dependency replaceable should declare 2 or 3.

The framework's 2 bracket verbatim: a dependency read inside the swap path. Unconditional, so a finding whose call kind the detector did not classify also scores 2 — the direction that does not understate risk.

dimensions.name: External liquidity exposure
dimensions.description: The hook moves tokens to external protocols, holds its own liquidity, or participates in lending flows.

brackets.label: Holds no balance between transactions
Holds fees or dust between transactions
Holds principal liquidity on behalf of users
Rehypothecates into an external protocol

dimensions.name: TVL potential
dimensions.measurableNote: Current TVL is observable on-chain in deployed mode and is reported as evidence, but the dimension asks about *potential*, which depends on incentive plans no tool can see.
dimensions.description: Liquidity can grow after launch. Hooks intended for farms or incentivized pools should assume higher potential TVL.

brackets.label: Under $100K (experimental or personal project)
$15M - $50M, mid-size protocol integration, or incentives
$50M+, major protocol integration, or significant incentives

dimensions.name: Team maturity
dimensions.measurableNote: Self-declared by definition. hookrisk has no defensible way to observe it and deliberately refuses to default it (error HR-E101).
dimensions.description: Experts with multiple production deployments and prior audits score low risk. New or anonymous teams score higher.

brackets.label: Highly mature: audited production deployments or UUPS upgrades across 2+ distinct codebases, mature DevOps, active incident response, demonstrated responsibility in past disclosures
Experienced: at least one audited production deployment or upgrade, some operational experience, less breadth across codebases
Moderately experienced: has deployed to production but without demonstrable operational maturity; upgrade, monitoring and incident processes informal or ad hoc
Unproven: no prior production deployments, or deployments lacking audits and operational rigor; new, anonymous, or no public track record

dimensions.name: Upgradeability
dimensions.description: Upgradeable hooks are more flexible but dangerous. Admin controls and proxy patterns introduce storage layout issues, logic upgrade errors, and governance attacks.
dimensions.interpretationNote: Graded by who controls the upgrade, which is what §5 of the framework's best-practice checklist actually cares about.

brackets.label: Immutable; no proxy, no DELEGATECALL to mutable code
Upgradeable behind a timelock
Upgradeable behind a multisig with no timelock
Upgradeable by an EOA, or a custom (non-standard) upgrade mechanism

dimensions.name: Autonomous parameter updates
dimensions.description: The hook adjusts its own configuration automatically or based on internal state. Autonomy amplifies misconfiguration and emergent behavior risks.
dimensions.interpretationNote: Graded by the guardrails the framework §1.6 requires: bounded rate of change, time/state gating, monotonicity.

brackets.label: All parameters set by an explicit privileged call
Self-adjusting within hard-coded bounds and a rate limit
Self-adjusting with bounds but no rate limit, or vice versa
Self-adjusting with neither bounds nor rate limiting

$comment_findingDerivation: HS-03 measures the *privileged* surface — who may change what — while
this dimension asks about *autonomy*. The two overlap where the
framework's guardrails do: a parameter that can move without bounds or
a rate limit. The mapping below is hookrisk's reading of that overlap,
and it is a floor in both branches: HS-03 cannot see a fee the hook
recomputes from its own state inside a callback, which is the shape the
3 bracket describes, so silence from HS-03 leaves the dimension
unmeasured rather than 0 (see derive.ts).

rules.rationale: HS-03 at HIGH is an unguarded state-changing external function: anybody can move the hook's parameters, so no access control enforces bounds or a rate limit. Scored 2 rather than 3 because the 3 bracket describes a hook that adjusts itself — here a caller still has to act — and never 0, because 0 is 'all parameters set by an explicit privileged call' and an unguarded call is not privileged.

HS-03 at MEDIUM is an owner-only mutator (hook-profile.hasOwnerOnlyFunctions). The framework's 0 bracket describes exactly this shape, but scoring 0 would rank a hook whose owner can move the fee level with a hook that has no parameters at all, and source analysis cannot see the owner's guardrails — timelock, ceiling, multisig. 1 records the surface as a floor without asserting autonomy; a team that has a timelock should declare 0 in hookrisk.toml.
An admin-surface finding below MEDIUM still evidences a parameter surface whose guardrails were not verified; the same floor applies.

dimensions.name: Price impacting behavior
dimensions.description: Hooks that directly influence the swap path, effective price, routing decisions, or fee structure.

brackets.label: Observes swaps; does not alter price, fee or delta
Charges a fixed, declared fee
Adjusts the LP fee dynamically within a declared ceiling
Returns a swap delta (custom curve or NoOp), or adjusts fees without a ceiling

$comment_findingDerivation: `custom-accounting` keeps its flat score in derive.ts (3, the bracket
verbatim). Only HS-06 needs a rationale recorded here, because the
number it produces is deliberately one bracket below the one its own
title suggests.

rules.rationale: HS-06's evidence is negative — it did not find a bound on a fee the hook sets dynamically. The 3 bracket ('adjusts fees without a ceiling') asserts that no ceiling exists anywhere, which a source detector cannot establish: a ceiling in the controller, in a library the detector did not resolve, or enforced off-chain is invisible to it. So the measured value is the 2 bracket, 'adjusts the LP fee dynamically', and the missing ceiling is reported as the finding itself. A reviewer who confirms there is no ceiling should declare 3.

$comment_tiers: Tier boundaries are stated explicitly in framework §3 and are not an
interpretation. The baseline recommendations are transcribed from the same
section; note that §3's 'optional' entries can be overridden upward by the
feature triggers below, which §3 does not say and FEEDBACK.md #4 reports.

tiers.name: Low Risk
tiers.summary: Relatively small surface area, little or no math, no external interactions.

tiers.name: Medium Risk
tiers.summary: Moderate complexity, custom logic, or meaningful dependencies.

baseline.detail: Where autonomy or parameter updates exist

tiers.name: High Risk
tiers.summary: Complex math, external liquidity, autonomous behavior, upgradeability, price impact, or large TVL.

baseline.detail: One of the two audits by a math specialist
Extended suite including invariants and stateful fuzzing: delta conservation, fee bounds, no unintended reentrancy, monotonicity of curve functions
With anomaly detection for silent failure modes
Invariant preservation, arithmetic bounds, reentrancy and callback-ordering assumptions, composite math correctness

monitoringTargets: Divergence between expected and actual deltas
Abnormal slippage patterns under small trade sizes
Deviations between theoretical curve output and on-chain execution
Drift in time-weighted or iterative math outputs

$comment_triggers: Seven feature triggers from framework §4. These fire independently of the
total score, which is the mechanism §5 relies on so that teams cannot score
themselves low while shipping dangerous primitives.
`derivedFrom` records how hookrisk decides a trigger has fired. The framework
does not define the relationship between its dimensions and its triggers
except for TVL; FEEDBACK.md #5 reports this and every entry marked
`interpretation: true` is our reading, not the Foundation's.

triggers.name: Custom Curve or Non Standard Math

requirements.detail: At least one audit including a math and invariants specialist
Validate intermediate steps, edge cases and input-range boundaries
Stateful fuzzing may significantly improve assurance

triggers.note: The framework states that a specialized math review is recommended whenever custom math is present, even at Low or Medium tier.

triggers.name: Hook Holds Its Own Liquidity or Manages External Liquidity

requirements.detail: At least one audit must evaluate liquidity flow correctness

triggers.note: The source says the trigger fires when the hook 'temporarily or permanently holds tokens'. Read literally that is nearly every hook, since take/settle within one callback holds tokens briefly. hookrisk reads it as holding a balance across transaction boundaries. FEEDBACK.md #10.

requirements.detail: Must review trust assumptions, failure modes and fallback logic

triggers.name: Autonomous Parameter Updates or Self-Tuning Hook

requirements.detail: Upgradeability must be minimized or time-locked
Debugging and recovery procedures must be documented
Auditors should simulate worst-case economic and adversarial price manipulation

triggers.name: Upgradeable
triggers.note: This is the one trigger the source ties unambiguously to its own presence: 'Triggers when any form of proxy or upgradeable logic exists.'

triggers.name: TVL 5 Rating

requirements.detail: At least one high quality audit regardless of feature set

triggers.note: Stated as a numeric threshold in the source, so no interpretation is needed.

$comment_actions: Display labels for the normalised action vocabulary. The framework phrases
the same action several ways across sections ('one full audit', 'at least
one high quality audit', 'at least one audit must evaluate liquidity flow
correctness'); collapsing them lets the merge rule work, while each
requirement keeps its original wording in `detail`.

actions.math-specialist-audit: Audit by a math and invariants specialist
actions.timelock-or-multisig: Timelock or multisig on privileged actions
